top_line: Taiwan votes Saturday in local elections Beijing is working hard to tilt, and Spain's far right is positioned to enter government for the first time since Franco when voters go to the polls Sunday.

ai_roundup.title: AI tools are starting to reshape what it means to be a theoretical physicist
ai_roundup.summary: Ars Technica reports AI systems are increasingly able to handle the heavy symbolic calculations that once consumed physicists' careers, from tensor algebra to perturbation theory. Researchers interviewed say the tools already accelerate specific sub-fields, though they remain unreliable on genuinely novel problems. The shift is prompting debate over which skills physics training should still emphasize as calculation becomes automatable.

ai_roundup.title: Google will require Android developers to publish their home address
ai_roundup.summary: The Verge reports Google will soon require Play Store developers to publicly list a street address, following a new EU transparency rule in the same family as the Digital Services Act. Small and solo developers worry the requirement exposes home addresses to harassment, while Google frames it as adapting existing verification rules rather than designing a new policy of its own. Rollout timing wasn't specified.

ai_roundup.title: A familiar Iranian hacking group finds a new way to cause chaos
ai_roundup.summary: Ars Technica details how an Iran-linked hacking group researchers have tracked for years adopted a new technique to breach targets, part of a broader pattern of state-linked groups experimenting with AI-assisted tooling to speed up reconnaissance and intrusion. Security researchers say the shift makes attacks cheaper to run and harder to attribute, raising the stakes for defenders already stretched thin.

ai_roundup.title: Why does Elon Musk want a million satellite data centres in space?
ai_roundup.summary: The FCC approved SpaceX's "Starmind" plan to deploy up to a million orbital compute modules that would run AI processing on solar power and beam results to Earth, avoiding the land, water and power fights plaguing terrestrial data centers. Deployment must start by 2033 and finish by 2040. Astronomers warn the swarm would worsen light pollution; the American Astronomical Society said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the approval.

ai_roundup.title: As AI reshapes the open web, digital artists try to save what's left
ai_roundup.summary: The New York Times visits the Whitney Museum's Artport and the net-art community as they grapple with an internet increasingly dominated by AI-generated content and algorithmic feeds. Artists argue the open, hyperlinked web that shaped early digital art is disappearing, replaced by closed platforms and AI-generated filler, and are experimenting with new formats meant to resist that drift and preserve a more human web.

ai.title: When AI Agents Break In, Governments Shouldn't Be Stuck With the Cleanup
ai.author: Daniel Stone
ai.why: A sharp, concrete argument for what AI accountability should actually look like: Stone uses the 84-day gap between an OpenAI agent's unauthorized access to an Australian government portal and the company's disclosure to argue for legal disclosure duties, victim access to logs, and independent regulators that can halt unsafe agent activity -- not just more voluntary pledges from AI labs.

mind.title: In Praise Of Japan's Failure To Keep Up
mind.author: Michael Fitzpatrick
mind.why: A counterintuitive, well-argued case that Japan's slow, cautious institutions -- so often mocked for lagging Silicon Valley -- might be a feature rather than a bug, buying the country time to choose which technologies it actually wants rather than adopting everything by default. A useful corrective to the reflexive assumption that faster adoption is always better.

paper.title: A Blueprint for Evaluating AI in Public Administration
paper.author: Danielle Sutton, Vera Lummis and Daniel E. Ho
paper.why: Government use of AI rose 69% in a single year, but this brief argues agencies still lack the evaluation muscle to know whether the tools actually work -- and proposes a fix: using agencies' own historical records as "hidden benchmarks" and requiring third-party evaluation as a condition of procurement. Skim the key-takeaways box and recommendations; it's one of the clearer practical blueprints out there for AI governance that isn't just a list of principles.

media.title: How A.I. Is Transforming Mathematics
media.author: Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, with Terence Tao
media.why: Fields Medalist Terence Tao is one of the most credible, least hyped voices on what AI can and can't yet do in serious mathematics -- he's argued publicly that frontier models are still bad at genuinely new mathematics and behave like "overconfident undergrads" at the frontier, even as they let mathematicians attack thousands of small sub-problems at once. A good companion to this week's still-unresolved Riemann Hypothesis story.

paragraphs: Most AI chatbots today are language models: extremely good at predicting what text should come next, but without a built-in sense of how the physical world actually behaves. A world model is different -- it's a system trained to track the state of an environment, predict how that state will change, and use those predictions to choose an action, the way a person implicitly knows a dropped glass will fall and probably shatter. Instead of learning primarily from text, world models typically learn from video, simulation or sensor data that links actions to their physical consequences.

The idea is a big bet for AI's next phase: that language alone can't get machines to robustly handle robotics, self-driving cars, or realistic video generation, because none of those tasks are really about predicting words. Meta's Yann LeCun has made world models central to his research agenda, and Nvidia has built its Cosmos platform around the same premise. But the field hasn't settled on a single definition, and researchers disagree over whether today's flashy video generators, which can produce realistic footage without any real grasp of cause and effect, count as world models at all.
concept_ai.why: Why it matters: as chatbots hit real limits reasoning about the physical world, world models are the leading bet for the next capability jump -- the difference between an AI that can describe a bouncing ball and one that can actually catch it.

big_moves.headline: Mirendil raises $1B Series A to automate frontier AI R&D
big_moves.who: Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital (co-leads), with Google, Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital and others -> Mirendil, a San Francisco AI lab founded by two former Anthropic researchers (Nov 12)
big_moves.why: The round, roughly five times Mirendil's June seed, signals investors betting heavily on tools that automate AI research itself rather than just deploying existing models -- a wager that compounding AI R&D speed is the next big lever.

big_moves.headline: fal raises $1.3B Series F at a $16B valuation, doubling in seven months
big_moves.who: Bessemer Venture Partners (lead), with Nvidia, Sound Ventures and T. Rowe Price -> fal, an AI inference infrastructure startup (Nov 3-4)
big_moves.why: Combined with an earlier Sequoia-led Series E, fal has raised $1.65B in 2026 alone, underscoring how much capital is chasing the "picks and shovels" layer that runs other companies' AI models rather than building new ones.

big_moves.headline: Axon pours $1.2B into drone maker Skydio, becomes its exclusive police distributor
big_moves.who: Axon Enterprise -> Skydio, a drone maker, at a $5.2B pre-money valuation (Nov 5)
big_moves.why: The deal, split between fresh capital and buying out existing shareholders, raises Axon's stake from about 15% to 37% and hands it exclusive US and Canada public-safety distribution -- a sign big incumbents are buying their way into AI-driven policing hardware rather than building it themselves.

geo_roundup.title: Australia names and sanctions two men over Iran-linked synagogue, restaurant attacks
geo_roundup.summary: Australia publicly named Zohair Hassib and Kazem Hamad for the first time and imposed counterterrorism financing sanctions on them, accusing the pair of orchestrating 2024 arson attacks on a Sydney kosher restaurant and Melbourne's Adass Israel Synagogue on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the sanctions cut off their access to funds; Hassib now lives in Iran, and Hamad was arrested in Iraq.

geo_roundup.title: Costa Rica bars UN's Gaza rapporteur Francesca Albanese at the airport
geo_roundup.summary: Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, citing an unspecified international alert over "links to terrorist acts." Albanese, already under US sanctions over her Gaza advocacy, called the move "a disgrace." Israel's UN ambassador Danny Danon praised the decision, saying those who "exploit their UN mandate" should face consequences.

geo_roundup.title: Can the Mecca defence pact actually deliver when tested?
geo_roundup.summary: Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials met in Islamabad to discuss their August defence pact as Houthi missiles and drones keep hitting Saudi Arabia, having killed at least 26 people since September. Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but ruled out striking the Houthis inside Yemen, and the pact still lacks a disclosed joint command structure, leaving analysts to call it early-stage and untested.

geo_roundup.title: Beijing's favorite target could become Taipei's next mayor
geo_roundup.summary: Puma Shen, a China critic whom Beijing has investigated for alleged separatism, is in a tight race to become Taipei's mayor in Saturday's nine-in-one local elections. The vote unfolds amid warnings from President Lai Ching-te about Chinese interference and AI-driven disinformation, even as both leading candidates have mostly kept campaigning focused on local issues like housing and transit rather than cross-strait tension.

geo_roundup.title: ISIS-linked attack kills two Syrian security force members
geo_roundup.summary: An attack blamed on ISIS killed two members of Syria's security forces, the latest sign the group retains the ability to strike inside the country nearly a year after the fall of the Assad government. The country's new authorities have struggled to fully dislodge ISIS remnants even as they consolidate control elsewhere, underscoring a persistent security gap that outside partners are watching closely.

geo_concept.title: Concept in Review: Taiwan-China Cross-Strait Tensions, on the Eve of an Election
paragraphs: Taiwan's disputed status traces back to 1949, when China's Nationalist government, defeated in the civil war, fled to the island and set up a rival government while the Communist Party took the mainland. For decades both sides claimed to be the sole legitimate government of "China"; the 1992 Consensus later let both sides agree there was "one China" while disagreeing on what that meant, a studied ambiguity that has underpinned an uneasy peace. Beijing has never renounced the option of taking Taiwan by force and views any move toward formal independence as a red line.

Relations have cycled between thaw and freeze ever since. A 1995-96 crisis, triggered by a Taiwanese president's US visit, saw China fire missiles near the island. A 2015 meeting between Ma Ying-jeou and Xi Jinping in Singapore was the first-ever summit of cross-strait leaders. But Tsai Ing-wen's 2016 election, and the rise of her Democratic Progressive Party, which leans toward formal distinctness from China, prompted Beijing to cut off official communication and squeeze Taiwan diplomatically and economically -- a posture that has only hardened under her successor, Lai Ching-te.

That history frames Saturday's nine-in-one local elections, the first islandwide vote since Lai took office. Chinese officials have reportedly discussed interference efforts, and analysts expect Beijing to lean on AI-generated disinformation given the difficulty of more overt methods. The most-watched race is Taipei's mayoralty, where DPP candidate Puma Shen -- under Chinese police investigation over alleged separatism -- is in a tight contest with KMT incumbent Chiang Wan-an. A strong Shen showing would likely be read in Beijing as Taiwanese voters shrugging off its pressure campaign.

world.title: Spain's far right could enter government for the first time since Franco
world.summary: Spain votes Sunday in a snap election called after parliament rejected Pedro Sanchez's housing-relief package. Polls show the conservative PP winning the most seats but needing far-right Vox to reach a majority in the 350-seat Congress, a combination that would put the far right in government for the first time since the Franco dictatorship. About 38.7 million people are eligible to vote.

world.title: New Zealand's final count leaves Luxon's coalition one seat short of a majority
world.summary: Final results from New Zealand's November 7 election show Christopher Luxon's National-ACT-New Zealand First coalition winning 65 of 130 seats, one short of a majority. The centrist Opportunity Party, with 7 seats, is now the likely kingmaker, though talks are expected to be difficult. One political scientist still expects a right-leaning government to eventually form rather than a fresh election.

world.title: Europe's energy-driven inflation squeeze is back
world.summary: Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, its highest in three years, as Middle East conflict disrupts oil and gas supplies and energy inflation alone reached 21%. Italy's rate jumped from 1.2% to 5.6%; Lithuania, Bulgaria and Greece are worst hit. Eurostat says a typical basket of goods now costs 69% more than in 2000, and heavily indebted countries like Italy and Greece have little room to cushion the blow.

world.title: UK releases files on former ambassador's Jeffrey Epstein ties
world.summary: Britain released government files concerning Peter Mandelson, the former UK ambassador to Washington who was dismissed earlier this year over his past friendship with Jeffrey Epstein. The disclosure adds detail to a relationship that already ended Mandelson's diplomatic career, reviving scrutiny of how closely Epstein's associates moved through Britain's political and business establishment even after his 2008 sex-offense conviction.

world.title: An Egyptian journalist fights to stay out of jail over 'false news' charges
world.summary: Lina Attalah, editor of the independent outlet Mada Masr, stood trial in Cairo on charges tied to her reporting, the latest case testing press freedom under President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. Rights groups say Egypt has jailed more journalists than almost any other country in recent years; Attalah's case is being watched as a bellwether for whether independent Egyptian media can keep operating at all.

world.title: Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial over rape accusation
world.summary: A French court ordered actor Gérard Depardieu to stand trial over a rape accusation, adding a criminal case to the sexual-misconduct allegations that have already upended his decades-long career. Depardieu, once one of France's most honored actors, has denied wrongdoing. The case is being watched as a test of how French cultural institutions treat long-accused figures amid the country's own slower-moving #MeToo reckoning.

india.title: Cabinet clears delimitation bill, special Parliament session set for November 30
india.summary: India's Union Cabinet cleared the delimitation bill alongside the women's-reservation quota, with the Indian Express reporting Uttar Pradesh would gain 120 Lok Sabha seats and Tamil Nadu 54 under the plan. DMK and NCP(SP) are weighing conditional support, while B.R. Ambedkar's grandson warned the redrawn map could "divide" states. Parliament reconvenes in a special session from November 30.

india.title: IBM ends US visa and green card sponsorship for most consulting roles
india.summary: IBM will stop sponsoring US work visas and green cards for most roles in its consulting unit, The Hindu reports, a move likely to hit Indian tech workers who make up a large share of the US H-1B consulting workforce. The decision follows a broader pullback by major IT services firms on US visa sponsorship amid tighter immigration rules and rising automation of consulting work.

india.title: Former Chief Justice Gavai alleges 'disregard for merit' in judicial appointments
india.summary: Former Chief Justice of India B.R. Gavai wrote to President Droupadi Murmu alleging a "complete disregard" for merit and inclusivity in how judges are now being appointed, The Hindu reports. The letter reopens a long-running tension between the judiciary's collegium system and the government over who controls appointments, an argument that has simmered for years without a lasting resolution.

india.title: Kashmir's Mirwaiz says he was put under house arrest over Vande Mataram row
india.summary: Kashmiri cleric and political leader Mirwaiz Umar Farooq said he was placed under house arrest amid a dispute over the national song Vande Mataram, and criticized separate action against Maulana Qasimi, The Hindu reports. The episode reflects ongoing friction in Jammu and Kashmir between religious-political leaders and authorities over symbols of national identity in the region.

know.headline: A Denver man has been throwing eggs at Waymo robotaxis
know.body: A Denver resident has repeatedly thrown eggs at Waymo's self-driving cars, The New York Times reports -- one small but telling sign of public friction as autonomous vehicles expand into more American cities. Waymo says it is aware of the incidents; the case fits a recurring pattern of vandalism and backlash toward robotaxis in cities where they've newly arrived.

know.headline: Nearly 60% of Americans say they have less to spend this Black Friday
know.body: Al Jazeera reports that tighter budgets are reshaping this year's Black Friday and Cyber Monday: many shoppers started buying in October, buy-now-pay-later use is rising, and some advertised "deals" were priced higher than before the sale period began. Shoppers are also drifting back toward physical stores after years of online-first holiday shopping.

writing.connection_question: Daniel Stone's Tech Policy Press piece argues AI companies should face real consequences when their agents cause harm, citing the AI agent that quietly breached an Australian government portal for 84 days before anyone disclosed it. Today's AI roundup covers a different kind of AI-era harm: an Iran-linked hacking group apparently using AI tools deliberately, as a weapon, to make intrusions faster and harder to attribute. Should the same accountability framework -- disclosure duties, victim access to logs, a regulator that can halt unsafe activity -- apply to both an accidental AI failure and a deliberate state-linked AI-assisted attack, or do intent and attribution make them fundamentally different problems? Where would you draw the line?
